section_summary: This section documents internal political turmoil in Japan from November to December 1931 surrounding the Manchurian Incident, culminating in the collapse of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and the establishment of the Inukai administration. It covers intelligence on the aborted October coup d'état attempt by army officers, the constitutional autonomy of the military from civilian oversight, and Home Minister Kenzo Adachi's political intrigue demanding a coalition government. Additional reporting examines Japanese public outrage over misinterpreted press statements by Secretary Stimson concerning military movements toward Chinchow and the new cabinet's immediate reinstitution of the gold embargo.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing report on rumors of an impending Japanese cabinet change.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet directs to file 793.94/2746 for Telegram No. 223 sent by Ambassador Forbes from Japan on November 18, 1931. The referenced telegram reports on rumors of an impending change in the Japanese Cabinet expected within the next few weeks.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 223 regarding Rumors of Impending Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting diplomatic assessments of Japanese internal politics and rumors of cabinet reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports discussions with the Dutch and Norwegian ministers in Tokyo, who caution that external pressure will consolidate public support for the Japanese military. He outlines three rumors regarding potential cabinet reorganization: an Adachi-Tokonami coalition, a pure Seiyukai cabinet, or a reorganized Wakatsuki coalition. The telegram also notes government press bans and military mobilization observed by Colonel McIlroy.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 223 from Tokyo (Impending Cabinet Change Rumors and Military Preparations)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing report on Ambassador Matsudaira's statement regarding Japanese internal conditions.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Telegram No. 762 from France, dated November 18, 1931, filed under 793.94/2758. It records a statement regarding internal conditions in Japan made by Japanese Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Statement on Internal Conditions in Japan by Matsudaira

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Dawes' report of information from Matsudaira on the situation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 235 filed under 793.94/2758, dated November 19, 1931. It relates to information conveyed by Ambassador Matsudaira to Ambassador Charles G. Dawes concerning internal Japanese developments.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Information Given Dawes by Matsudaira Regarding Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing warnings of political plots and potential assassinations of Japanese leaders.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 229 filed under 793.94/2792, dated November 20, 1931. It notes that political assassinations and plots are common during intense political excitement in Japan, with rumors marking Shidehara, Makino, Wakatsuki, Ikki, and Inoue as potential targets.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Plots and Political Assassinations in Japan

subfiles.about: Despatch detailing an aborted military coup d'état planned for October 17, 1931.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes relays reliable intelligence derived from Metropolitan Police records regarding an army conspiracy discovered on October 11, scheduled for execution on October 17. The conspirators, primarily army majors and captains allied with Katsumaro Akamatsu of the Social Democratic Party, intended to assassinate key civilian leaders and establish a military dictatorship under Prince Chichibu. The involved officers were briefly confined or transferred rather than formally prosecuted to prevent public outrage and military discontent.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 382: The Aborted Coup d'État of October 17, 1931

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the constitutional independence of the Japanese military and the rise of chauvinistic public sentiment.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes examines the fundamental structural reasons for the civilian government's inability to restrain the Imperial Japanese Army. The Army General Staff possesses direct access to the Emperor on strategy and tactics, allowing it to bypass the Cabinet and precipitate ministerial collapses by withholding a War Minister. The despatch also details the growing influence of junior officer factions and reactionary nationalist groups, including youth and student patriotic societies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 383: Military Autonomy and the Weakness of Civilian Control in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 382 regarding the October coup plot.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes Ambassador Forbes' Despatch No. 382 concerning the discovered army coup d'état attempt. It reviews the conspiracy to install Prince Chichibu as dictator, the planned assassinations of cabinet ministers, the targeting of the Asahi and Hochi newspaper offices, and the quiet release of the arrested military officers.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Tokyo's Despatch No. 382 on the Planned Coup d'État

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Home Minister Adachi's public agitation for a coalition cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that Home Minister Adachi issued a statement calling for a coalition cabinet upon his return from inspecting military maneuvers. Press reports indicate that Adachi intends to resign from the ministry, an action likely to force the dissolution of the entire Cabinet due to his extensive political following.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 232 from Tokyo: Adachi Advocates Coalition Cabinet

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting Forbes' report on the impending Japanese cabinet crisis to Ambassador Dawes in Paris.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State transmits the verbatim text of Ambassador Forbes' Tokyo Telegram No. 232 to Ambassador Charles G. Dawes in Paris for his information. The quoted telegram describes Home Minister Adachi's advocacy of a coalition government and his anticipated resignation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 597 to Paris: Transmitting Tokyo Report on Adachi's Maneuvers

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that the immediate cabinet crisis has subsided and highlighting internal army dissent.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that Home Minister Adachi has temporarily subsided and that the immediate cabinet crisis appears to have passed. He notes that radical younger officers in the military are strongly at odds with conservative superiors like the War Minister and Chief of Staff. Additionally, Dr. Rudolf Teusler shared that prominent elder statesmen recognize that junior army elements have gotten dangerously out of hand.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 247 from Tokyo: Passing of Immediate Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Dawes' report on the temporary subsiding of the Japanese cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 613 from France filed under 793.94/2966, dated December 1, 1931. It notes reporting on the Japanese cabinet crisis which appeared to have passed for the time being.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Telegram No. 613 regarding Japanese Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Shidehara's statement regarding ongoing political attacks against him.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 249 from Japan, dated December 2, 1931, filed under 793.94/2989. It records Foreign Minister Shidehara's statement that domestic political attacks against his policies are continuing.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Shidehara's Statement on Continuing Political Attacks

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch analyzing the political dynamics, party factions, and potential successors in the cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes provides a detailed analysis of the forces driving rumors of a cabinet change despite the Minseito's parliamentary majority. He details political intrigues between Home Minister Adachi and Seiyukai factional leader Takejiro Tokonami aimed at establishing a coalition government. He reviews potential alternative prime ministers, including Tsuyoshi Inukai, Baron Tatsuo Yamamoto, and Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma, and discusses rumors of a potential Imperial Rescript designed to curb military independence.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 396: Rumors of an Impending Cabinet Change in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing the October coup attempt and civilian government control over the military.
subfiles.summary: This Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviews Tokyo Despatches Nos. 382 and 383 concerning the suppressed October coup attempt and the institutional autonomy of the Japanese military. It summarizes the constitutional roots of the military's direct access to the Throne, the resulting discrepancies between diplomatic statements and field operations, and the spread of chauvinistic sentiment among the Japanese public.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Reported Coup d'État in Tokyo and Military Control by Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing report of Forbes' conversation with Count Kabayama on government instability.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Despatch No. 388 from Japan, dated November 12, 1931, filed under 793.94/3109. It relates to a conversation between Ambassador Forbes and Count Kabayama regarding the structural weakness of the Japanese Government and its impending collapse.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 388 on Conversation with Count Kabayama

subfiles.about: Despatch enclosing memoranda of conversations with Baron Shidehara and Count Kabayama on the Manchurian conflict and government weakness.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes transmits memoranda of confidential discussions held with Foreign Minister Shidehara and Count Aisuke Kabayama. Shidehara discussed conditions for troop withdrawal, Chinese local peace preservation committees, and intense friction with Chang Hsueh-liang. Count Kabayama confided that the Wakatsuki Government was tottering due to economic failures and military insubordination, explaining the historical ascendancy of the military class and warning that foreign pressure would only harden Japanese national resolve.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 388: Conversations with Baron Shidehara and Count Kabayama

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the resignation of Prime Minister Wakatsuki and his Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that Prime Minister Wakatsuki formally tendered the resignation of the Cabinet to the Emperor on the afternoon of December 11, 1931. The collapse was precipitated directly by Home Minister Adachi's refusal to cooperate unless a coalition cabinet was formed. Either Wakatsuki (reconstructed) or Seiyukai president Tsuyoshi Inukai is anticipated to be commanded to form the next government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 258 from Tokyo: Resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi regarding the cabinet resignation and boycott rumors.
subfiles.from: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.summary: Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi discuss the newly announced resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and its relation to the League of Nations resolution passed in Paris. Stimson directly questions Debuchi regarding allegations by Henry Cabot Lodge that the U.S. had given assurances it would not employ an economic boycott against Japan. Debuchi unequivocally confirms that Stimson had never given any official or personal assurance of that nature and writes a direct signed denial on the inquiry.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Secretary Stimson and Japanese Ambassador Debuchi

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the ministerial composition of the newly formed Seiyukai Cabinet under Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes lists the full ministerial appointments of the new Seiyukai Cabinet formed under Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai, who also serves as Acting Foreign Minister. The roster includes Korekiyo Takahashi as Finance Minister, Lieutenant General Sadao Araki as War Minister, Admiral Mineo Osumi as Navy Minister, and Takejiro Tokonami as Railway Minister. The Foreign Affairs portfolio is noted as being reserved for Ambassador Kenkichi Yoshizawa upon his return from France.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 261 from Tokyo: Formation of the Inukai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing telegram reporting Inukai's summons to form a cabinet and awaiting foreign minister appointment.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 259 from Japan, dated December 12, 1931, filed under 793.94/3179. It notes that diplomatic action regarding alleged Chinese promises to withdraw from Chinchow must await the appointment of a new foreign minister and that Inukai will likely form the cabinet.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Appointment of New Foreign Minister and Chinchow Issue

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Inukai's summons to the Imperial Palace to form a new government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that following the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet, diplomatic representations must await the designation of a new foreign minister. He confirms that Seiyukai President Inukai has been summoned to the Imperial Palace to receive the imperial mandate to form a new administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 259 from Tokyo: Inukai Summoned to Form Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing reports that Mitsui financial interests backed Adachi's maneuvers leading to cabinet fall.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Telegram No. 263 from Japan, dated December 14, 1931, filed under 894.51/313. It relates to rumors that Mitsui financial interests backed Home Minister Adachi's political maneuvers to force a cabinet resignation, followed by Adachi and three key supporters resigning from the Minseito.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Mitsui Backing of Adachi's Political Moves

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting alleged financial speculation by Mitsui interests behind the cabinet fall and the reimposition of the gold embargo.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports rumors that Mitsui interests purchased enormous quantities of U.S. gold dollars (estimated up to two hundred million) and financed Adachi's political maneuvers to topple the Cabinet. The newly installed Inukai Cabinet immediately reinstituted the embargo on gold exports, securing massive profits for currency speculators. Adachi and three prominent associates have formally severed ties with the Minseito.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 263 from Tokyo: Mitsui Interests and the Gold Embargo

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing despatch on Japanese domestic political reactions to Secretary Stimson's Chinchow statements.
subfiles.summary: This document file note references Despatch No. 407 from Japan, dated December 4, 1931, filed under 793.94/3271. It indexes reporting on internal political repercussions in Japan arising from Secretary Stimson's statements regarding an understanding to halt military operations against Chinchow.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 407 on Political Conditions Following Stimson's Statement

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting severe domestic political fallout and press reaction against Shidehara and Kanaya following Stimson's Chinchow statement.
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Neville reports on the domestic repercussions in Japan resulting from misreported press accounts of Secretary Stimson's November 27 press conference regarding military restraint toward Chinchow. Although public anti-American hostility subsided after official clarifications, the Seiyukai opposition and House of Peers factions aggressively attacked Foreign Minister Shidehara and Army Chief of Staff General Kanaya for alleged violations of the Military Secrets Law. The despatch encloses full English translations of editorials from the Tokyo Jiji, Hochi, Chugai Shogyo, and Nichi Nichi.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 407: Domestic Repercussions of Secretary Stimson's Statement Regarding Chinchow

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing the underlying causes of the Wakatsuki Cabinet's resignation.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Ambassador Forbes' Telegram No. 258 regarding the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet. It attributes the fall of the ministry to Home Minister Adachi's personal dissatisfaction and coalition demands, budgetary difficulties coupled with pressure to restore the gold export embargo, and mounting complications from the Manchurian crisis.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet
